clinicalPearls: A rare sex-cord stromal tumour of young women that classically produces androgens, causing progressive virilisation: oligomenorrhoea or amenorrhoea, hirsutism, acne, clitoromegaly, deepening of the voice and loss of female body contour.
Preceding defeminisation (breast atrophy, cessation of menses) often heralds the androgenic phase, and symptoms may regress after resection of a localised tumour.

Tumours are graded as well, moderately or poorly differentiated, and a subset contains heterologous elements (most often mucinous epithelium or, less commonly, cartilage or skeletal muscle) or a retiform pattern.

A significant proportion, especially those with a retiform pattern or heterologous elements in young patients, harbour DICER1 mutations, prompting consideration of the hereditary DICER1 syndrome and its associated tumours.
Serum testosterone is characteristically raised while dehydroepiandrosterone sulphate is usually only mildly elevated or normal, helping to distinguish an ovarian source from an adrenal one.
Immunohistochemistry typically shows positivity for inhibin, calretinin, SF-1 and often FOXL2, with Leydig cells sometimes highlighting crystalloids of Reinke.
Most are unilateral and confined to the ovary at diagnosis, so fertility-sparing unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy is appropriate for well-differentiated, stage-confined disease in young women.

Prognosis correlates strongly with differentiation and stage: well-differentiated tumours are effectively benign, whereas poorly differentiated or ruptured tumours carry a real risk of recurrence and metastasis.
reference.pathophysiology: Sertoli-Leydig cell tumours are sex-cord stromal neoplasms composed of Sertoli cells, Leydig cells and, in less differentiated forms, primitive gonadal stroma recapitulating testicular development in the ovary. The Leydig cell component secretes androgens, chiefly testosterone, producing the virilising syndrome; some tumours instead secrete oestrogen or are hormonally silent. Many arise on a background of germline or somatic DICER1 mutation, which impairs microRNA processing and predisposes to this and other DICER1-associated tumours, particularly in the young and in tumours showing retiform or heterologous differentiation. Degree of differentiation reflects how closely the tubular Sertoli architecture is preserved; poorly differentiated tumours show sarcomatoid stroma, mitotic activity and loss of organised tubules, and correlate with a more aggressive, potentially metastatic course.
additionalDifferentials: steroid (lipid) cell tumour of the ovary
additionalInvestigations: serum total testosterone and free androgen index
serum dehydroepiandrosterone sulphate to help localise the androgen source
transvaginal pelvic ultrasound and MRI of the pelvis
CT of abdomen and pelvis for staging in higher-grade disease
DICER1 mutation testing on tumour and consideration of germline testing
redFlags: rapidly progressive virilisation suggesting an androgen-secreting neoplasm rather than functional hyperandrogenism
markedly elevated serum testosterone with a palpable or imaged adnexal mass
tumour rupture with haemoperitoneum or an acute abdomen
poorly differentiated histology or extra-ovarian spread indicating aggressive potential
personal or family history suggesting DICER1 syndrome, such as pleuropulmonary blastoma or thyroid nodular disease
reference.prognosis: Well-differentiated tumours are essentially benign and cured by conservative surgery, whereas moderately and poorly differentiated tumours, those with heterologous mesenchymal elements, and ruptured or advanced-stage tumours carry a substantial risk of recurrence and metastasis with correspondingly poorer survival.
pitfalls: Attributing hirsutism and menstrual disturbance to polycystic ovary syndrome and missing a virilising tumour when testosterone is disproportionately high.
Failing to consider and test for DICER1 syndrome in young patients or those with retiform or heterologous tumours.
Assuming an adrenal source without checking that dehydroepiandrosterone sulphate is not markedly elevated.
Underestimating a poorly differentiated tumour by sampling only well-differentiated areas.
Rupturing the tumour intra-operatively, which upstages the disease and worsens prognosis.

management: For well-differentiated, stage-confined disease in a young woman, fertility-sparing unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy with surgical staging is usually curative.

For advanced-stage or poorly differentiated disease, or tumours with heterologous mesenchymal elements or rupture, total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy and surgical debulking is the surgical standard.
Lymphadenectomy can reasonably be omitted from staging surgery in the absence of grossly enlarged nodes.
Adjuvant systemic therapy is reserved for higher-risk histology or advanced disease extent, not used routinely after complete resection of low-risk tumours.
Adjuvant platinum-based combination chemotherapy is used for poorly differentiated tumours, heterologous mesenchymal elements, tumour rupture, or advanced stage disease.
Hormonal therapy with a gonadotropin-releasing hormone analog is a reasonable option in advanced or recurrent disease, particularly when further surgery or cytotoxic therapy is not suitable.
Radiotherapy is not considered a standard part of management for this tumour type.
Virilising features often regress, at least partially, once the tumour is resected.
Surveillance should combine clinical review with serial androgen markers (serum testosterone) and pelvic imaging (ultrasound or MRI) to detect recurrence.
Germline DICER1 mutation testing and genetic counselling should be considered, particularly in young patients or those with retiform or heterologous histology.

Refer to a gynaecological oncology multidisciplinary team for surgical staging decisions, especially when weighing fertility preservation against completeness of staging or when histology is poorly differentiated, heterologous, or ruptured.
Refer for genetics assessment when DICER1 syndrome is suspected.

Advanced or recurrent disease, or disease being considered for gonadotropin-releasing hormone analog therapy, should be managed by a gynaecological oncology team rather than in general gynaecology follow-up.
